item.title: From the Spear to the Server
item.description: Sometimes common men have more power and society tends to be more open and democratic and sometimes power becomes concentrated in the hands of elites so society becomes more authoritarian. The power pendulum has swung throughout the centuries as men went from carrying spears to carrying IPhones. In primeval life, men were roughly equal militarily. There was no government or large organization of society. A man with a spear could defend himself. He could kill another man or a mammal without a king or warlord to command him.

item.title: The Man Who Named Downing Street
item.description: When a regime falls, most of the people who served it fall with it. A small number do not. George Downing served Cromwell’s Commonwealth and then, without missing a step, served the restored monarchy that hanged his former comrades. Reinhard Gehlen ran Hitler’s military intelligence on the Eastern Front and within two years was running an intelligence service for the Americans. Hossein Fardoust stood beside the Shah of Iran as a lifelong confidant, then reappeared inside the Islamic Republic’s own security apparatus.

item.title: The Statute, the Harem and the Regent Mother
item.description: In 1558, the Scottish reformer John Knox published a tract: The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women. His argument was that a woman ruling over men violated natural and divine order. Knox was not a crank shouting into the void. He was articulating a real strand of Reformation political theology, and he was writing when a run of women had ended up holding or wielding power across Europe: Mary I of England, Mary of Guise as regent of Scotland, Mary Stuart on the Scottish throne, Margaret of Parma governing the Netherlands, Jeanne d’Albret in Navarre — building on a slightly earlier generation of Margaret of Austria, Louise of Savoy, and Isabella of Castile, who had already shown a woman could rule a major power outright.

item.title: Living Is Not For The Weak
item.description:
‘Living is not for the weak’, says Anatoly Knyazev to Oliver Queen in the Arrow drama series.

Life is a struggle. It is hard so be hard. But that is what makes you strong. Adversity is the making of the Arrow. Oliver Queen transforms from being the spoilt son of a billionaire to superhero Arrow who wreaks revenge on the wealthy criminal class who ruin his home Starling City. This is a modern fairy-tale based on a truth known since the beginning of history. We can review how this has been framed over the millennia by taking two men who set their thoughts on paper (or parchment) and left us their perspectives.

item.title: Spies, States and Secrets: Intelligence from Moses to Stalin
item.description:
Spying is probably the world’s second oldest profession.

In the Old Testament, Moses and Joshua sent spies into Canaan, the Promised Land. This did not go quite to plan for Moses as 10 out of his 12 agents had their own agenda and were against the idea of invading Canaan. They had little faith and said it was too dangerous despite evidence that God was on their side. He parted the Red Sea so they could escape from Egypt. The other two agents reported that it was entirely possible. This preparation for the invasion of Canaan ultimately paid off when Joshua successfully took it.

item.title: Caesar, Turing and Satoshi
item.description: I hold cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Solana and Avalanche partly as a hedge against inflation and partly because I have a libertarian streak which makes me fantasize that I can be independent of traditional finance and the moguls of Wall Street. I do not keep them on an exchange because part of my libertarian idea is that I should control the cryptocurrency assets and not the exchange. Of course, this means that I am completely responsible for their safe-keeping and I cannot blame an exchange if they disappear.

item.title: How to order beer in Prague (if you are not Czech)
item.description:
The Vltava river runs through Prague and alongside the river there is a promenade and quay where boats and boat hotels moor. The wall above the promenade has bars which are set inside and open out to the promenade with huge circular doors which can swivel open on warm days.

I was sitting outside one of these bars with my son, and next to us there was a large part of young German men. What struck me when the Czech waitress came to take their orders was that they had to speak to her in English. Germany is the huge neighbor to the north of the Czech Republic and, under the Hapsburgs, Prague used to be a predominantly German-speaking city. I might expect that German would be the second language but a series of momentous historical accidents over hundreds of years dictated that it would not be.
